title: Projectile motion
objectives: Resolve a launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
Treat horizontal and vertical motion independently, linked only by time.
Calculate time of flight, maximum height and range.
Describe qualitatively how air resistance changes a trajectory.

explanation.heading: Two independent motions
body: Ignoring air resistance, the only force on a projectile is its weight, which acts straight down. So:

• Horizontally there is no force: the velocity uₓ = u cos θ stays constant.
  • Vertically the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards: use the suvat equations with u_y = u sin θ.
The two motions are completely independent. The only thing they share is time, so most problems are solved by finding the time from one direction and using it in the other.

explanation.heading: Key results on level ground
body: time to the top = u_y / g maximum height H = u_y² / 2g
time of flight T = 2u_y / g range R = uₓ T = u² sin 2θ / g

The range is largest when sin 2θ = 1, at θ = 45°. Complementary angles such as 30° and 60° give the same range. At the top, the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not, and the acceleration is still g.

explanation.heading: Adding air resistance
body: Drag acts opposite to the velocity and grows with speed (roughly as v²). It has a horizontal component, so uₓ is no longer constant.
Compared with the vacuum parabola: the maximum height is lower, the range is shorter, and the path is not symmetric: the descent is steeper than the ascent. The best launch angle drops below 45°.
There is no neat formula for this case. The IB only asks for the qualitative effect; the numbers come from a step-by-step simulation (see the extension topic on numerical models).

demo.intro: The dashed curve is the vacuum parabola; the solid one includes drag. Change the launch speed, angle and drag coefficient.
notice: Set drag to zero and the two curves coincide.
With drag on, the descent is visibly steeper than the climb.
The best angle (shown on the range plot) moves further below 45° the faster you launch.

examples.title: Launch on level ground
examples.problem: A ball is kicked at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal on level ground. Find the time of flight, the range and the maximum height. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

steps.why: v² = u² + 2as with v = 0 at the top.

examples.title: Horizontal launch from a cliff
examples.problem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from the top of a 45 m cliff. How far from the base of the cliff does it land?

steps.do: Vertically: u_y = 0, s = 45 m, a = 9.81 m s⁻²
steps.why: 'Horizontally' means the vertical component starts at zero.
Fall time is the same as if the stone were simply dropped.

takeaways: Resolve, then treat each direction separately; time is the link.
At the top v_y = 0, but vₓ ≠ 0 and a = g.
Air resistance lowers the height, shortens the range, breaks the symmetry and lowers the best angle.
